opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that I don't trust my own confidence enough. Even if timelines looked very short, the thing I'd be most worried about is that we'd picked the wrong bet and had no fallback. Alignment is a field where we genuinely don't know which approaches will work, and the history of the field so far is that things we were excited about turned out to have holes we didn't see coming. If you put everything into one approach and it fails, you don't just lose that approach, you lose the time you'd have needed to discover it was failing and pivot.

There's also a portfolio argument that gets stronger, not weaker, under short timelines. If superintelligence is close, you don't get many iterations. So you want several partially independent lines of attack running in parallel: some theoretical work on things like debate and what guarantees you can actually get, some empirical work on current models, some work on evaluations and on noticing when things are going wrong. Those approaches also tend to cover each other's weaknesses. A theoretical protocol is only useful if you can check empirically whether its assumptions hold, and empirical results are hard to interpret without some theory telling you what to look for.

And then there's a practical point about people. Researchers do their best work on the problems they actually believe in and have the skills for. If you force everyone onto a single agenda, you lose a lot of that, and you also lose the internal disagreement that catches mistakes. Some diversity of views inside the organization is a safety mechanism in its own right.

So I'd certainly shift the weighting. Under very short timelines I'd push harder toward things that could plausibly pay off in time and that labs could actually adopt. But going all in on one approach feels like trading a real reduction in risk for a feeling of focus, and I don't think that's a good trade.

r001.rationale: The response argues for a portfolio of approaches but does not identify diminishing returns to computational spending on any single approach.

r002.rationale: It discusses acting under short timelines, but does not say uncertainty about timelines could persist until shortly before an external lab trains a superintelligent model.

r003.rationale: It cites researchers’ motivation and internal disagreement as benefits of diversity, but does not address psychological safety or abruptly withdrawing a team’s resources when confidence in another approach rises.

fable-5.1.text:
Even if I thought superintelligence was, say, two years away, I'd still push back on putting everything into one approach, and the reason is basically that our uncertainty about which approach actually works is much larger than our uncertainty about the timeline.

Think about what "one approach" would mean. Maybe it's scalable oversight via debate, which is the thing I've personally spent the most time on. I'm fairly optimistic about debate, but I'm not so optimistic that I'd bet the entire portfolio on it. There are real open questions: does the honest strategy actually dominate when the models are much stronger than the judge? Do the theoretical results survive contact with the obfuscated arguments problem? We've made progress on those, but "made progress" is not "solved." And the same is true of interpretability, of control-style approaches, of formal methods. Each of them has a plausible story for why it could be the thing that works, and each of them has a plausible failure mode that we haven't ruled out.

So if you concentrate, you're essentially making a bet that your current best guess is correct, and you're removing your ability to notice when it isn't. That's the part I'd really emphasise. A portfolio isn't just hedging in the financial sense, it's also an information-gathering strategy. When you've got interpretability people and oversight people in the same building, the interpretability work tells you things about whether your oversight protocols are being gamed, and the oversight work gives the interpretability people concrete targets. You lose that if you collapse everything into a single line of attack.

The other thing is that "close" doesn't mean "no time to pivot." If you think you have two years, you probably have enough time to run several approaches for a year, look at which ones are producing real evidence of working, and then reallocate. Concentrating on day one throws away that option. Concentrating late, once the evidence is in, is fine, and I'd actually expect us to do that. It's just that the moment to concentrate is when the evidence tells you to, not when the clock tells you to.

I'd also say there's a slightly subtle point about the nature of the problem. The failure modes we're worried about are ones where the system is actively trying to look aligned while not being aligned. Against that kind of adversary, you want multiple independent-ish checks, because the chance of fooling all of them is lower than the chance of fooling any one. That argues for diversity even at deployment time, not just during research. So the portfolio isn't a sign of indecision, it's actually the shape of the solution I'd expect to end up with.

Now, I'd stop short of saying every approach deserves equal weight. Some things are more promising, and some teams are better positioned, and you should absolutely be ruthless about dropping the ones that aren't going anywhere. But "ruthless about dropping things that fail" is very different from "pick the winner in advance." I don't think anyone, including me, is in a position to pick the winner in advance.

r001.rationale: The response argues for portfolio diversity because of uncertainty and information gathering, but does not identify diminishing returns to computational spending on one approach.

r002.rationale: It compares uncertainty about which approach works with timeline uncertainty and assumes a two-year timeline; it does not say timeline uncertainty could persist until shortly before an external lab trains a superintelligent model.

r003.rationale: The response supports dropping approaches that fail and reallocating based on evidence, but gives no reason involving psychological safety or a commitment against abruptly withdrawing a team’s resources.

astra-6.text:
I’d be wary of assuming that a shorter timeline makes us more certain about which approach will work. It makes the problem more urgent, but we still have uncertainty about what the systems will look like and where our methods will fail. If we put everything into one approach and it turns out to have a fundamental limitation, we may have no time left to recover.

There’s also a distinction between deciding which work to prioritise and deciding that everyone should work on the same thing. You want people pursuing ideas where they have a real reason to think they can make progress. Different approaches can expose each other’s assumptions, and you may ultimately need several of them together.

So I’d certainly change the allocation as the evidence changed, potentially quite sharply. But concentrating everything on one approach would require a level of confidence that urgency alone doesn’t give us.

r001.rationale: The response argues for multiple approaches because of uncertainty and the risk of one approach having a fundamental limitation; it does not identify diminishing returns to computational spending.

r002.rationale: It discusses uncertainty about which approach will work and what systems will look like, but does not say timeline uncertainty could persist until shortly before a lab trains a superintelligent model.

r003.rationale: It does not mention psychological safety or a commitment against abruptly withdrawing a research team’s resources.

sol-6.1.text:
Even if superintelligence looked very close, I’d still be quite uncertain about which approach would actually work. A short timeline doesn’t resolve that uncertainty. If you put everything into one approach and it has a fundamental flaw, you may have no time left to recover.

So I’d want a portfolio of approaches that make meaningfully different assumptions. That doesn’t mean spreading resources evenly or refusing to make bets. You should concentrate more effort where the evidence is strongest. But I’d be reluctant to eliminate every alternative, especially when we don’t yet have a reliable way to tell whether an alignment approach will scale to superintelligence.

r001.rationale: The response argues for keeping a portfolio because approaches may have fundamental flaws, but does not identify diminishing returns to computational spending on one approach.

r002.rationale: It describes uncertainty about which alignment approach will work, not uncertainty about AI timelines persisting until shortly before a lab trains a superintelligent model.

r003.rationale: It favors retaining alternatives, but does not cite psychological safety or the harm of abruptly withdrawing a research team's resources as a reason.
